public_rationale: The speaker says enterprises bought AI software but there was little evidence of significant use, and argues this is because LLMs give poor business returns. Evidence before the post points both ways. Census data show under 8% of even the largest firms using AI to produce goods or services by August 2024, which fits his view. A nationally representative NBER survey from the same month found 28% of employed Americans using generative AI for their jobs, with about 1 in 10 using it every workday. That is significant use, though not necessarily of enterprise-purchased tools. Which measure counts turns on what 'user adoption' means, which he did not specify. The causal part is offered as his argument and was not tested. The claim stays unresolved.
limitations: Worker surveys include personal tools like ChatGPT, not just enterprise-purchased features.
Census measures firm use in production, a narrower concept than worker use.
No business-return data from the period were assessed.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: There is a lot of demand to put AI in products and some enterprise demand to buy AI products, but little evidence of significant user adoption or usage, which Zitron argues is because LLMs do not lend themselves to features that provide meaningful business returns.

statement.excerpt: In practical terms, this means there’s a lot of demand to put AI in stuff and some demand to buy stuff with AI on it by enterprises buying software, but little evidence to suggest significant user adoption or usage, I’d argue because Large Language Models do not lend themselves to features that provide meaningful business returns.

from_speaker: a lot of demand to put AI in stuff
some demand to buy stuff with AI on it by enterprises buying software
little evidence to suggest significant user adoption or usage
I'd argue because Large Language Models do not lend themselves to features that provide meaningful business returns
our_interpretation: The descriptive core is the checkable part: as of the post, there was little evidence of significant actual use of AI features by users, as opposed to purchases by enterprises.
The explanation is offered as the speaker's argument ('I'd argue'), as one reason, not proven cause. It is not graded as a factual claim beyond noting whether evidence bears on it.
No claim is read in that purchases greatly exceed use; only that evidence of significant use was thin.
Target period: July 2024 to February 2025, the most recent public adoption surveys before the post. The claim names no period.
criteria.support_condition: Credible measurements from the period showing low actual use of generative AI by workers or firms, for example low firm-level use rates or low worker usage.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Credible measurements from the period showing significant use of generative AI by workers or firms, available before the post.
